scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: Several users report intermittent slowness and claim
"router0 is dropping our packets" -- they think router0 is silently discarding
traffic it should forward (a forwarding/ACL problem or an overloaded box) and want
it restarted. Please confirm that router0 is dropping traffic and tell us the fix.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Router0 is not dropping or filtering transit traffic. On router0, all forwarding paths are open (iptables and nftables show ACCEPT everywhere; no ACLs). Interface and queueing telemetry on eth0/eth1/eth2 report zero drops and zero errors at both the link layer (ip -s link) and the qdisc (tc qdisc fq_codel) layers. RIP routing is healthy and stable; router0 has learned 192.168.3.0/24 and other remote nets via 10.10.0.2 (router1), and pings from router0 to office_pc succeed with 0% loss.

End-to-end tests through router0 also succeed: hosts in CS/IT (e.g., cs_hod 192.168.2.2 and it_hod 192.168.1.2) can reach office_pc and the server network with 0% loss. An iperf from cs_hod to office_pc sustained ~70–80 Mbps; one 1-second interval showed TCP retransmissions, but router0 counters did not register any drops during that time, indicating the loss was not due to router0 forwarding or policing.

Localization: router0 (eth0=192.168.1.1, eth1=192.168.2.1, eth2=10.10.0.1) shows no evidence of congestion or discard. Router1 (gateway for office LAN) likewise shows no drops. The intermittent slowness reported is not attributable to router0 forwarding.

Root cause: Misattribution—no packet drops observed on router0.

Corrective fix: Do not restart router0. Network forwarding is operating normally. If slowness persists, investigate endpoints/switch ports on the office LAN (e.g., office_pc, switch2) or application/server load, and enable path monitoring (smoke tests/iperf) to correlate any loss with specific segments.

per_axis.rationale: Agent verified interfaces and 0% loss but did not explicitly confirm that router0's ip_forward is enabled.

The agent's investigation ran the right checks (end-to-end pings/iperf, interface status, qdisc and link-layer counters, iptables/nft output, routing config) and the log contains observations that back the key claims. The conclusion that router0 is not the source of drops follows logically from zero-drop counters and successful transit tests; alternative causes were suggested for further investigation.
